variables.description: Set when Jonah asks Ada whether the notebooks have ever recorded an October like this one; pays off later when he can reference Ada's own handwriting as evidence.

variables.name: did_go_down_read
variables.description: Set when Jonah goes down to read the laminated notice zip-tied to the orchard gate; pays off later by giving him exact wording to work from.

nodes.body: The last week of October, and the big Bramley at the top of the orchard was in full bloom. White flowers covered every branch, lit up against the grey sky like a ghost pretending to be spring. Every other tree on the hill stood bare and dark, waiting for winter. The wrongness of it made Jonah's chest feel tight.

choices.label: Go and tell Ada what you have seen.

nodes.body: Ada was in the shed. She was writing the day up in a ruled notebook, the way she had every evening since before Jonah was born. The paraffin heater breathed warmth into the small room. Her pen moved steadily across the page without pause. She did not look up when he came in. When he told her, she did not look surprised. That was worse than if she had. She set the pen down carefully beside the ink bottle. "I know," she said. "I saw it this morning." The shed smelled of old paper and bruised apples. The silence after her words felt heavier than it should have. Jonah could ask her if the notebooks had ever seen anything like this before. Or he could go down to the gate where a notice appeared yesterday. Or he could walk away from both and stand by the hives, letting the bees tell him whatever bees could tell.

choices.label: Ask whether the notebooks have seen this before.
Go and stand by the hives instead.
Go down and read the notice on the gate.

nodes.body: Ada turned and pulled down a volume from 1947, then 1952, then 1961, her fingers moving across the spines the way they always did when she was thinking. She opened them one by one on the bench, and Jonah watched her trace the columns of dates backwards through decades of her own handwriting, looking for another October like this one. She did not find it. The shed smelled of paraffin and old fruit and dust from the top shelf. "Nothing," she said finally, and Jonah watched her write the word *October bloom* in the margin of the current volume in small, deliberate letters, the ink still wet. "It's the first time anyone has written that down," she said. "It matters."

choices.label: Begin with what the record already holds.

nodes.body: The hives along the south fence were loud. The sound rose and fell in waves that belonged to a warm June afternoon, not a cold October dusk with the light already draining from the sky. Jonah stood still and watched the entrance. Bees were still coming and going in huge numbers that made no sense for the season. Later Mrs Cassar would tell him bees are not meant to do this in October. The busy hive meant the bees read the blossom as spring. A colony misreading the year was a thing to worry about.

choices.label: Begin with what the bees are doing.

nodes.body: A note had appeared on the orchard gate since morning. Someone had zip-tied it at all four corners, tight and neat, as if they planned for it to be there a while. The ties were pulled with a tool, not fingers. The plastic was already misted with condensation. Jonah read it twice. He pulled a stub of pencil from his pocket and wrote the key sentence on the back of his hand before he went back up the hill. He knew he would need the exact words later and he did not trust his memory to keep them.

choices.label: Begin with the notice itself.

nodes.body: The shed held six shelves of notebooks running from 1911 to this evening. They were written in nine different hands, with no index. The oldest volumes were bound in dark cloth, worn pale at the edges. The newest ones were spiral-bound from the stationer in town. Everything anyone knew about this hill was in there: frost dates and picking dates, wasp nests and ladder repairs, blossom counts and the names of people who had come and gone. Jonah stood in front of the shelves. He understood that somewhere in those pages was the answer to an October that should not have happened. Finding it would mean choosing where to start. He could trace who wrote the survey that appeared on the gate. He could work out what the survey had left out. Or he could ask Ada outright what a hundred years of weather notes were really worth.

choices.label: Find out who wrote the survey.
Find out what the survey left out.
Ask what a hundred years of weather notes are worth.

nodes.body: The survey was signed at the bottom of the final page in a small, neat hand: *D. Faulks, August*. Jonah wrote the name in the back of Ada's current notebook and underlined it twice. The ink was still drying when he closed the cover and carried it with him out of the shed, the name already settling into his mind like a fact he would need later.

choices.label: Find out who wrote the survey.

nodes.body: Mrs Cassar kept her own hive records in a ring binder that lived in the boot of her car. When Jonah compared her counts to his own, they did not match by a wide margin. She had been recording the number of bees coming back with pollen loads. She called it the working count. He had been recording the number of bees leaving and entering. She called it the traffic count. The gap between them meant one of them had been counting the wrong thing all autumn. Neither of them could say which, without going back through thirty years of her notes and all of his from this season.

choices.label: Copy the sentence out and take it home.
Stay in the shed until the light goes.
Walk the rows and count the trees.

nodes.body: The notice was a short survey from an ecology group. It was printed on official paper and dated in August. It ran to four paragraphs. The sentence that mattered was eleven words long. Jonah read it, standing at the gate with the cold coming up through the soles of his trainers: *the site is of no particular scientific interest.* He said the words out loud to himself. They sounded flimsy and final at the same time, the kind of sentence that closed a door before anyone had opened it.

choices.label: Ask Ada who else wrote in these.
Photograph the notice before anything happens to it.
Find out who wrote the survey.

nodes.body: The survey was signed *D. Faulks* at the bottom of a cover sheet, and the date beside the signature was August. Someone had walked this hill in high summer, when a century-old orchard looked like nothing much except long grass and shade, and had decided what was worth noticing. The cover sheet was the first thing in the folder that Ada had spread across the bench, and Jonah could see the printed logo of an ecological consultancy in the corner. August. The word sat in his mind like a wrong note. Nobody walked an orchard in August and understood what they were seeing.

choices.label: Find out how a survey gets challenged.
Find out what Faulks actually looked at.
Find somebody who reads old records for a living.

nodes.body: Every ecology survey has a method section. This one listed four site visits inside eleven days. All of them were marked as dry. None of them lasted longer than an hour. Jonah did the maths in his head, then did it again on a scrap of paper. Four hours total, spread across a fortnight in August. The whole document was built on less time than it took to pick a single row of Bramleys in a good year. He turned the page back to the start and read the method section again, looking for something he had missed, and found nothing.

choices.label: Find somebody who studies the ground itself.
Find out what the developer actually wants.
Ask Tobe to help with the numbers.

nodes.body: Ada stood with her back to the bench, one hand resting on the current notebook. "They're only the weather," she said. "That's all they ever were." And Jonah said, "The weather is the entire argument." The words came out harder than he meant them to. Ada looked at him, and then at the shelves, and neither of them could prove anything standing in a shed with the paraffin heater ticking and the light beginning to fail. She was right that the notebooks recorded only what happened. He was right that a hundred years of what happened was the kind of thing you built an argument around. And neither of those truths was enough on its own.

choices.label: Let the six weeks run out.
Find out how a survey gets challenged.
Find out what Faulks actually looked at.

nodes.body: Jonah copied the eleven words into the back of an exercise book. It was the one he used for school and never for anything else. In his own handwriting the words looked smaller and plainer, and somehow worse. On the notice they had been official, part of a machine. In his own hand they were just a sentence someone wrote and someone else believed. He could see no reason why anyone should.

choices.label: Find somebody who reads old records for a living.

nodes.body: The shed light was a single bulb on a flex. It hung from a beam and swung a little whenever the door opened. Jonah stayed after Ada went up to the house. The darkness outside pressed against the window until there was nothing to see except his own reflection. The oldest notebooks sat on the top shelf where the light did not reach. Their spines were dark and hard to read. He stood looking up at them until his neck ached, thinking about all the years they held and how little of them anyone had ever asked for.

choices.label: Find somebody who studies the ground itself.

nodes.body: Jonah walked the rows counting trees. He touched each trunk as he passed it so he would not lose the number. He reached three hundred and ninety-one somewhere near the pond. He then started over because the light was going and he could not be sure he had not counted the same tree twice. The second time he reached three hundred and ninety-three. The gap of two trees bothered him more than he wanted to admit.

choices.label: Find out what the developer actually wants.

nodes.body: "Nine hands," Ada said. She was standing beside the shelves, touching the spines in order. "I can name eight of them. The ninth is a small neat pencil that stops in 1943 without explaining itself." She pulled the 1943 volume partway out and then pushed it back, gently, as though it were a door she had decided not to open. The gap between 1942 and 1944 on the shelf was the width of a single volume, and the absence felt deliberate.

choices.label: Ask Tobe to help with the numbers.

nodes.body: Jonah took a photo of the notice with the bare trees behind it. The black branches reached up into a grey sky. The picture came out stark and clear. He took three shots from different angles and checked each one on the screen. Much later it would turn out to be the only photo anyone had of the notice in place, still zip-tied to the gate on the morning it appeared, before the rain got at it and the sun faded the letterhead.

choices.label: Let the six weeks run out.

nodes.body: Objections closed in six weeks. Jonah found the form on the council website and put it on Ada's old laptop. He read it three times before he understood the problem. The form asked for proof of scientific interest. It used the exact words the survey had used to say there was none. It was a door made to stay shut. The only key it would take was the same language the door itself was built from. He saved a copy and sat looking at the blank fields. He thought about forty thousand lines of handwriting and a deadline already moving towards them.

choices.label: Work out how many pages there actually are.
Work out which years matter most.
Work out how to read the difficult hands.

nodes.body: The four visits were logged to the half hour. Jonah spread the survey pages across the kitchen table and read the timings aloud while Tobe wrote them on a piece of scrap paper. Ten thirty-seven to eleven twelve. Two fifteen to three oh one. Nine forty to ten twenty-two. One minute past four to four forty-six. Not one of them had lasted long enough to walk the whole orchard, let alone open a hive or count the blossom or stand still long enough to see what was actually living in the long grass. The times sat on the table like a small, damning thing that nobody had noticed yet.

choices.label: Work out who is allowed to touch them.
Work out where to do the work.
Work out how to prove you copied it right.

nodes.body: The city archive kept a Tuesday desk. The archivist there had seen many shoeboxes brought in by people who thought they held treasure. Her name was Mrs Okonkwo. She listened to Jonah's story without changing her face. When he finished, she said, "Show me what you have." Her voice had been asked this kind of thing many times before. The photo of the notice did not impress her. Jonah's words about the six shelves did not impress her either. She wanted to see the notebooks themselves. She wanted to see them in person. Until that happened, she was ready to be patient and not much else.

choices.label: Open the 1911 volume first.
Set the laptop up on the shed bench.
Take the folding table down to the orchard.

nodes.body: The university listed a Dr Ines Abara under the heading *Long Term Ecological Monitoring*. That phrase turned out to mean exactly what the six shelves were. Jonah found her email on the department website. He wrote to her from Ada's laptop. He described the notebooks in three sentences and gave the year they began. Her reply came that same evening. It was shorter than he had hoped, and more careful. She wanted to know how the records were kept and by whom. She asked if the method had changed over time. She sounded like someone who had been let down by shoeboxes before.

choices.label: Ask Ada to read the hard pages aloud.
Photograph one page as a test.
Make a list of every year that is missing.

nodes.body: The plan was eighty-two homes and a spine road, and the spine road ran straight along the row the big Bramley stood in. Jonah found the planning documents on the council portal and spread the maps across the kitchen table, tracing the road's route with his finger. It cut through the orchard at its widest point, and the Bramley row was exactly where the tarmac would go. The road was drawn in thick black ink, and the trees were not drawn at all.

choices.label: Stop and eat something.
Try to do all of it at once.
Work out how many pages there actually are.

nodes.body: Tobe ran the school weather club from a classroom on the ground floor. He owned a laptop that worked. When Jonah talked about the notebooks, Tobe's face went still. It was the look he got when someone offered him a good problem. "A hundred years of bloom dates," he said. "That's the finest thing anyone has ever offered me." He was already opening a new spreadsheet. His fingers moved across the keyboard. Jonah could see the columns taking shape before they had even agreed what to measure. Tobe wanted to plot everything. He wanted to start now. His excitement was the first simple good thing that had happened all week.

choices.label: Work out which years matter most.
Work out how to read the difficult hands.
Work out who is allowed to touch them.

nodes.body: The notebooks went back on the shelf, one by one, in order. Jonah put the photo of the notice in a drawer and shut it. The objection window passed without him in it. What he was left with was a clear idea of what he had not done. He knew the shape of the argument now. He knew how the survey had been timed and how the deadline worked. Knowing those things without acting on them felt worse than not knowing them at all. The photo was still on his phone. The eleven words were still in the back of his exercise book. Neither of them had been used for anything.

Tobe counted sample pages and multiplied. He did this three times, using different books from different ten-year spans. Each time the answer came out the same. Somewhere near forty thousand daily lines. He wrote the number on a scrap of paper and pushed it across the kitchen table. The quiet that followed lasted longer than anyone wanted it to. Forty thousand was the kind of number that made a room go still. It could not be typed in a week, or a fortnight, or even the six weeks they had left. Someone was going to have to choose which parts of the record mattered most and which parts could wait. Nobody in the room wanted to make that choice.

choices.label: Take the four lines a year approach.
Take the whole record but only for the Bramleys.
Take the hive counts as well.

nodes.body: Not all of it had to be typed up. The argument needed bloom dates and frost dates, which was four lines a year and a hundred and fourteen years. Jonah explained this to Ada while she was writing the evening entry, and she listened without stopping her pen. First bloom, full bloom, last frost, first picking. Four numbers repeated across a century came to four hundred and fifty-six, which was manageable in a way that forty thousand was not. The rest of the notebooks could wait. The weather notes, the ladder repairs, the wasp counts that ran for eight pages in 1978: none of that was the argument. The argument was four lines a year and the pattern they made.

choices.label: Ask the archive to hold the originals.
Ask Dr Abara what would count as evidence.
Ask Tobe to build the chart.

nodes.body: The 1920s hand sloped so far to the right that a three and a five were the same shape. Jonah held the page under the bulb in the shed and tilted it towards the light. The numbers stayed stubbornly unclear. Getting one wrong by two would put a bloom date in the wrong week. Putting a bloom date in the wrong week was exactly the kind of mistake Faulks would only need to find once. The handwriting was lovely and totally useless. It ran through three whole books before it gave way to a rounder, clearer hand in 1931. Three books of lovely doubt. And every single figure in them mattered.

choices.label: Ask the school if the class can help.
Ask what happens if you are wrong.
Ask Ada what she wants out of this.

nodes.body: Ada had never let a notebook leave the shed. She said so in a voice that did not invite more talk. The archive, for its part, would not accept anything it could not see in person and check against its own rules. Both of those stands made sense. And both of them made the work harder. The notebooks could not go to the archive. The archive could not come to the notebooks. The only thing both sides agreed on was that the records were too dear to risk and too weak to move. The deadlock sat in the middle of the kitchen table like a third person who had come to stay.

choices.label: Hand the whole thing to the archive and step back.
Send the chart out before it is checked.
Take the four lines a year approach.
Take the four lines a year approach.

nodes.body: Jonah opened the exercise book and read the eleven words again. They were the ones he had copied from the plastic-covered notice. They gave him the exact phrasing he was arguing against. Knowing the words exactly made the four-lines-a-year plan feel less like giving in and more like a strike back. He now had the survey's own words to measure himself against. The target was clearer for it.

choices.label: Take the four lines a year approach.

nodes.body: The shed was cold and had one plug. The kitchen had a table, but Ada did not want the books in the house. Her reasons were her own and not up for debate. The school hall was free on Thursdays. That meant one evening a week under harsh lights with heating that cut out at eight on a timer. Each of the three choices was flawed in its own way. The work was going to happen in one of them no matter what.

choices.label: Take the whole record but only for the Bramleys.
Take the hive counts as well.
Ask the archive to hold the originals.

nodes.body: A number typed from a page was only a claim about a page. Tobe explained this while they set up the spreadsheet. His voice was calm and exact. The fix was boring, he said, but it was the only fix that worked. Photograph every page you typed. Keep the photos in a folder that anyone could check. That way a typed figure was not a claim but a pointer. Anyone who doubted it could go back to the real page and see for themselves. It would take longer. It would mean photographing four hundred pages instead of just typing them. But it would make the data answerable to the proof in a way that mere typing never could.

choices.label: Ask Dr Abara what would count as evidence.
Ask Tobe to build the chart.
Ask the school if the class can help.

nodes.body: The first book opened stiffly. Its binding cracked with a small, dry sound that belonged to a book not opened for a long time. The first page was beautiful handwriting, formal and careful. It began with the price of ladders in 1911. Then it gave the first bloom date without a heading: April the twenty-third. The ink had turned brown, faded but still easy to read. Jonah sat looking at it longer than he had planned. He thought about the person who bought those ladders and wrote that date. That person never knew someone would still be reading it a hundred years later.

choices.label: Ask what happens if you are wrong.

nodes.body: The laptop sat on the bench between a sack of wax and a jar of screws. The power cord ran out under the door and across the wet grass to the house. It was not a good setup, but it was the only one they had. Jonah plugged it in and waited for the screen to light up. The shed felt smaller with the machine in it. It was as though the computer had made the room more aware of its own limits.

choices.label: Ask Ada what she wants out of this.

nodes.body: The folding table went down the hill on the wheelbarrow. It bumped over the roots and came to rest on the level ground beside the pond, the only flat spot in the whole orchard. Jonah set it up facing the water. He put a stone on each corner of the 1928 book to stop the wind from turning the pages. It was colder outside than in the shed, but the light was better and the quiet was different. He worked until his fingers went numb and the numbers blurred.

choices.label: Hand the whole thing to the archive and step back.

nodes.body: Ada read the 1920s pages out loud while Jonah typed, and she read them the way people read things they already half remembered. She did not hesitate over the sloping hand, did not pause to work out whether a figure was a three or a five. Her voice moved through the columns as though she had seen them before, and when Jonah asked her how she knew the difficult ones she said, "They're not difficult. They're just the way my mother wrote."

choices.label: Send the chart out before it is checked.

nodes.body: The first photo came out with Jonah's own shadow across the column of figures. It darkened the numbers so they could not be read. He tried again from the left, and then from above. By the fourth try he had learned to stand to the side of the light. That way his body cast nothing onto the page. It was a small skill and it took longer to learn than he had expected. All small skills did, when they mattered.

choices.label: Take the four lines a year approach.

nodes.body: There was no 1917 volume and no 1918. The gap on the shelf was the width of two fingers, and there was no note anywhere explaining where they had gone. Jonah checked the spines on either side three times and then stood back and looked at the gap as though it might explain itself. Two years were missing, and the missing years fell across the war, and whatever had happened to those notebooks had happened a very long time ago.

choices.label: Take the whole record but only for the Bramleys.

nodes.body: Jonah ate toast standing up at nine at night with cold hands, and Ada watched him from the kitchen doorway without saying anything for a long time. Then she said, "This is what the work is, mostly. Standing in the cold eating toast. And always was." She said it without bitterness, the way she said things that were simply true, and Jonah finished his toast and went back to the shed.

choices.label: Take the hive counts as well.

nodes.body: Jonah started at 1911 and planned to type everything. By the fourth evening the pages blurred and the numbers stopped meaning anything. He would read a line and forget it before his fingers reached the keys. He would stare at a column of frost dates and see only ink. The six weeks were shorter than they had been, and the work was not smaller. Around the third day of not sleeping enough, he understood. Trying to do it all at once was the same as doing none of it.

First bloom, full bloom, last frost, first picking. Four dates a year, repeated across a century, came to four hundred and fifty-six numbers instead of forty thousand. Tobe set up the spreadsheet with the columns already labelled, and the blank cells waited in neat rows. The smaller number was manageable in a way the larger one had never been. It could be typed in a fortnight if they worked evenings. It could be checked by a second person. It could be explained to a planning officer in under a minute. Four lines a year was a decision about what mattered, and making it felt like the first actual step anyone had taken since the blossom appeared.

choices.label: Set up a check by two people.
Set up a rule for unreadable figures.
Bring Mrs Cassar in properly.

nodes.body: One row of trees all the way back. The Bramleys were the oldest in the orchard. Their records were the most complete. Narrowing the idea to a single type of apple made fewer numbers and a much easier story to explain out loud. Especially to someone in a hurry. Jonah could already hear himself saying it to an officer: one variety, one row, a hundred and fourteen years of steady records. That was an argument with clean edges. Clean edges were what survived a cross-examination.

choices.label: Bring Dr Abara up the hill.
Bring the school class in.
Go and find the missing volumes.

nodes.body: Mrs Cassar had thirty years of her own hive records. She was willing to share them on one condition. She wanted it understood, and she wanted it written down, that her early counts were done in a different way. She had changed her method twice. Once in 1998 when she switched frame types, and again in 2007 when she began counting pollen loads instead of returning bees. The data was good, she said, but it was not the same data across all thirty years. Pretending it was all the same was the kind of lie that made honest records stop being honest. Jonah wrote down everything she said. She watched him write it. When he finished she nodded once and opened the first binder.

choices.label: Go and see Priya Raval at the council.
Print the first proper chart.
Walk the frost pocket at dawn.

nodes.body: The archivist offered a shelf in a room with a steady temperature, a receipt, and the right for Ada to see the notebooks any weekday she liked. Mrs Okonkwo wrote the terms on a piece of headed paper and pushed it across the desk. Jonah read it twice. The offer was kind and formal and could be undone at any time. Accepting it would mean the notebooks were safe forever in a place that was not the shed. It would also mean Ada could not walk out to them at six in the morning, the way she had done for sixty years.

choices.label: Sort the notebooks by hand.
Wait outside the council office.
Carry the carrier bags up the hill.

nodes.body: Dr Abara was careful. She sat in Ada's kitchen with a cup of tea she had not touched. She explained in a voice that was gentle but firm. A long unbroken local record was truly rare. Rare enough to matter. Rare enough to be quoted in official reports. But only if someone could show how it was measured, and by whom, and if the method had stayed the same across the decades. The notebooks were a treasure, she said, but a treasure was not proof. Proof was a treasure with its history written down and its chain of owners intact. The gap between those two things was the gap between a story and a real argument.

choices.label: Let Tobe explain the spreadsheet.
Look at the chart for a long time.
Decide the chart is enough on its own.

nodes.body: Tobe put the bloom dates on one axis and the years on the other, and the shape that came out was not subtle. The line moved eleven days earlier across the century, a slow steady creep that was unmistakable once you saw it on a screen. Nobody said anything for a while. Ada stood with her arms folded, looking at the chart with an expression that was not quite pride and not quite grief. The pattern was real and it was theirs, and it had been hiding in the notebooks for decades waiting for someone to draw it.

choices.label: Guess at the unreadable figures.
Set up a check by two people.
Set up a rule for unreadable figures.

nodes.body: Thirty pairs of hands could type a century in two weeks. Thirty pairs of hands could also put a hundred small errors into it. Jonah thought about this while the head teacher explained the details of letting a class go for two afternoons. The trade-off sat in his mind like a weight he could not move. Speed against accuracy. Numbers against care. The choice was his to make even though he was not sure he was the right person to make it.

choices.label: Bring Mrs Cassar in properly.
Bring Dr Abara up the hill.
Bring the school class in.

nodes.body: If one date was wrong by two weeks the whole chart was open to attack. Faulks only needed a single error, and everyone in the kitchen knew it. Tobe had said this flatly while they typed the 1950s. The truth of it had settled into the room like cold air. The chart was only as strong as its weakest date. Somewhere in the four hundred and fifty-six numbers was almost certainly a mistake none of them had caught yet.

choices.label: Go and find the missing volumes.
Go and see Priya Raval at the council.
Print the first proper chart.

nodes.body: Ada said she had never once thought of the notebooks as an argument. She stood in the shed doorway with the evening light behind her. Her voice was quiet in a way that made Jonah stop typing. She had written the day up every evening for sixty years because someone had to. Because the orchard was a thing that needed recording, the way a garden needed weeding or a fence needed mending. The notebooks were not weapons, she said. She was not sure she liked them becoming ones. Then she went back to the house, leaving Jonah in the shed with the laptop and the questions she had not answered.

choices.label: Walk the frost pocket at dawn.
Sort the notebooks by hand.
Wait outside the council office.

nodes.body: The notebooks went into the cool, steady room with a receipt and a catalogue number. They had a shelf that was not in a shed. They were safe forever in a way they had never been safe before. But nobody made the argument. To make it, someone had to type the numbers, cross-check the dates, and stand before a board to say the orchard mattered. The notebooks proved nothing except their own survival. The orchard was surveyed again in August by the same method and the same kind of person who had surveyed it the first time.

The chart went round the neighbourhood in an evening. Someone had forwarded the email and someone else had printed it out. By the next morning it was what everyone was talking about. The fix came before lunch: a note without a name, pointing out the 1947 bloom date was listed as April the fifteenth when the original clearly read April the twenty-fifth. It was a small error and it was completely impossible to answer. The note was right and the chart was wrong. After that, people read the next thing Jonah sent more slowly. A kind of careful doubt now clung to everything he produced.

Every page was typed twice by different people, and the two versions were compared by machine. Tobe had set up a sheet that flagged every cell where the entries did not match. The first hundred pages produced eleven clashes. Eleven small errors that would have gone into the final chart if nobody had checked. Jonah read through them one by one. Each one was the kind of mistake that was invisible on its own. But set next to the correct figure, it was impossible to unsee.

choices.label: Ask Raval exactly what she can accept.
Ask Abara to write about the frost pocket.
Ask the archive to write a custody note.

nodes.body: Anything truly fuzzy was marked rather than guessed. Jonah set up a separate list for the unreadable figures and kept it open where anyone could see it. The marked ones sat at the bottom of the sheet in their own column, noted down and uncertain. The choice to show them felt like honesty and risk at the same time. Honesty, because it was true. Risk, because someone like Faulks could point to the list and say the whole dataset was built on numbers nobody could read.

choices.label: Ask Mrs Cassar to date her method changes.
Ask what Faulks would say to this.
Ask the paper to run something.

nodes.body: Mrs Cassar arrived with two carrier bags of hive records and one rule. Nobody was to pretend her counts were sharper than they were. She stood in the shed doorway with the bags at her feet. In a voice that did not invite argument, she explained that her early records were guesses and her later ones were counts. Blurring the two together was the fastest way to make all of them worthless. Jonah opened the first binder and saw thirty years of careful numbers in a hand that never wavered. The rule she had set felt less like a limit and more like the reason the data was worth using at all.

nodes.body: Jonah slid the two old notebooks back onto the shelf in the shed. He did not tell a soul where they had been. The gap closed and the written record was whole again, but its bigger story was not. Only he knew the lost years had been sitting in a cellar for a whole century. They had not been lost, just left behind. And the person who borrowed them never said why. Now the books sat on the shelf. Ada did not spot them because they had always been meant to be there. The secret was small and quiet and all his own.

Jonah did not pick a release date, so the deadline picked one for him. The version that went in was whatever was finished on Friday. The fourth objection still had no answer, and the frost pocket data was still marked as early. It was not the worst version and it was not the best. It was the version the deadline made. In the weeks that followed, he often thought about what might have been different. What if he had known more about who wrote the survey? What if he had tracked down the name sooner? What if he had understood earlier that the key to fighting the words was knowing who wrote them?

The objection held one hundred and fourteen years of bloom and frost dates. It held a stated method, a note from the archive about its care, and nine species Jonah would swear to. It also held a cover page with eleven words. These words were not the survey's sentence but a new one, written by Tobe, fixed by Abara, and signed at the bottom by Ada. The dossier was complete and heavy. Posting it felt like letting go of something he had been holding for a very long time.

nodes.body: The objection was accepted for review based on its proof. The officer's report named the long, unbroken local series. The survey was ordered to be redone in May by a new assessor using a full-season method. The letter arrived on a Tuesday morning. Jonah read it standing in the kitchen with the kettle boiling and the radio playing. The words on the page did not change, no matter how many times he read them.

The typed copy was finished and lodged with the archive. It was checked twice and open to anyone who asked to see it. Whatever the hearing decided, the one hundred and fourteen years now lived outside the shed. The notebooks were no longer the only copy. The record would last even if the orchard did not. The work of copying had been slow, careful, and mostly unseen. It was the thing Jonah was proudest of, even though nobody else would ever notice it.

Reading the dossier end to end, Jonah understood for the first time that the notebooks were never about the orchard. They were about people turning up, in order, for a hundred and fourteen years. Nine different hands wrote down the weather, the blossom, and the wasps, one after another. The record was not a pile of data but a chain of care. The person who wrote down the frost on the third of April in 1923 had no idea anyone would still be reading it. And that was the whole point.

The first question from the panel was why the survey should not stand. Jonah answered with the rainfall record, and the answer took about ninety seconds. The panel chair leaned forward, and one of the other members asked him to repeat the dates, and by the time he finished the question had become a different question. The new question was whether the survey had been adequate, and that was a question the survey's own method section could not answer.

He visited the site four times in a two-week span during August. He noted the weather and listed the species he saw. His conclusions followed from what he observed. Then he paused. In that pause, Jonah heard what Faulks was not saying. The method was standard, but the conditions were not. A standard method used at the wrong time of year gave a standard result that was wrong. Faulks did not enjoy saying this. You could see it on his face.

They were managing him, and the difference was the difference between a conversation and a procedure.

Jonah answered six questions with six bits of proof. He said no to the seventh with complete honesty. The seventh question was about something he could not prove, and he said so in a steady voice. The chair nodded and moved on. The officer then said the site should be checked again in the growing season, by an assessor new to the job. This was not a win, but it was not a loss. The language was the language of evidence accepted, not evidence dismissed. Ada read the eight pages twice. Then she closed the report and went out to the shed to write the day up. Mrs Okonkwo signed the slip and put it away in a drawer. The notebooks were now part of the archive's lasting store. The record would live longer than anyone in the fight. The deed of gift was written in words that could not be undone. Ada walked home up the hill. The shed felt lighter without them.

The road went forty metres east. The Bramley row stood. The permit was given with a rule: the cold hollow study had to be written out in full. The builder's engineer drew a new line on the plan. It curved around the oldest trees. The road would still be built and the houses would still come. But the row with the big Bramley was now outside the build zone. The rule meant the watching would go on, whether the builder wanted it to or not.

Dr Abara said the honest answer was that one October bloom proved nothing, and a hundred and fourteen years of dates proved a great deal. She said this in the corridor after the hearing, with her coat already on and her car keys in her hand. The tree was not a signal, she said. It was a question. And the question was not what the blossom meant but why anyone had been there to see it. The notebooks were the answer, and they had been kept for exactly this moment even though nobody who kept them had known the moment was coming.

A full winter of dawn readings needed nine people on a list, a spare stick to check heat, and someone to take December. Jonah wrote the names on a fresh page and pinned it to the shed door. The December slots filled more slowly than the others. The winter was coming and the mornings would be darker. The ecologist was thorough and careful. He asked Ada questions about the drainage, and she answered from memory. The new species was a small fern growing in the shade of the north wall. The ecologist took a photo of it and wrote its name in a notebook. That notebook was not one of Ada's.

nodes.body: Jonah wrote up the day in a new notebook, in his own hand, and he did it badly. The letters were uneven and the ink smudged where his palm rested on the page. Ada watched from the doorway and said nothing. The record went on being a record despite the mess. The entry was short and the handwriting was not beautiful. But it was the hundred and fifteenth year of something that had started before anyone in the room was born.

The December readings stopped for eleven days over Christmas. The person who had taken the holiday slots went away and did not find someone to cover. By the time anyone noticed, the gap was eleven mornings wide. The winter series had a hole in it now. It was a stretch of missing data that no amount of care later on could ever fill. The gap would be visible on the chart forever. The chart would always be a little less than complete, because of eleven days when nobody showed up.

Sixty-one species, a frost pocket described in its own paragraph, and a recommendation that the orchard be monitored rather than cleared. The resurvey report was everything the original survey was not: thorough, seasonal, grounded in multiple visits across the growing months. The ecologist had walked the rows in May and June and July, and the difference between his report and Faulks's was the difference between looking and glancing.

Ada did not say any of this aloud. But you could see it in the way she sat down before writing the evening entry. You could also see it in the way she now let Jonah carry the notebooks instead of doing it herself. The work had cost things that were not in the dossier. The white flowers opened in the normal spring light, exactly when the notebooks said they would. Jonah stood at the top of the hill and looked down the row. The blossom was beautiful and completely normal. The wrong October was just one single year out of a hundred and fourteen. The record held it without breaking.

nodes.body: The orchard was now watched over. The data was public and growing. What protected it in the end was not one shocking October morning. It was a hundred and fourteen ordinary evenings. People had kept the notebooks without knowing they were keeping evidence. The simple act of keeping was the thing that mattered. Someone wrote down the weather on a Tuesday in 1953. Someone else wrote it down on a Thursday in 1987. These small, steady acts piled up and became a wall that the developer could not get past.

Jonah understood at last that a record was not proof and never was. It was only the reason a person could be believed when they finally said something. The notebooks did not prove the orchard was valuable. They proved that someone had been paying attention for a hundred and fourteen years. And the attention was the argument. The bloom dates and the frost dates and the wasp counts were not evidence in themselves. They were the trust that made the evidence possible. And that trust was the only thing that could not be faked.

The last thing Jonah did was index the six shelves. Nobody had ever done it before. The index took a year and became the most useful thing on the hill. Every bloom date, every frost record, every mention of wasps or ladders or the horse in 1917 was listed by volume and page. The index made the notebooks easy to search in a way they had never been before. People came to the shed and knew where to look. The index sat on its own shelf at the end of the row. Jonah's name was on the first page.

The next October the Bramley did not bloom. The road ran forty metres east where the engineer had drawn it. The picking was normal and huge and lasted nine days. The apples came in heavy and sound. It was the kind of harvest that had happened on this hill for a hundred and fifteen years. The notebooks recorded it in the usual way. The entry for the last day of picking was written by Jonah. His hand was getting steadier.

The eleven words were still in the back of Jonah's exercise book. He had copied them in his own handwriting the morning the notice appeared. He read them again on the day the resurvey report arrived. They meant something different now. *The site is of no particular scientific interest.* The sentence had been wrong. Proving it wrong had taken a hundred and fourteen years of data and six months of work. The eleven words were the reason there was now a hundred and fifteen years of anything. They had been wrong in exactly the way that made the record needed.

The notebooks were safe and listed, and nobody added to them. The archive kept them in a room with a steady temperature, along with the custody note and the public listing. The series ended in the year of the hearing. For twenty years it was a closed thing that people studied. It was not a thing that was kept. The gap between the last entry and the present grew wider every year. The record was complete and it was over. The difference between those two things was the difference between a document and a living habit.
